reading: See how the excellent painter has made the Trojan boy
carried through the highest stars by the bird of Jupiter.
Would anyone believe that Jupiter was touched by love for a boy?
Tell me, where did the Maeonian old man [Homer] invent this?
Counsel, mind, and joy in God — the one to whom these are given
is believed to be snatched up and to stand before highest Jupiter.

greek.translation: “To rejoice in counsels”, Ganymede [the name is explained from the Greek words].

2.motto: Human wisdom is folly before God.

reading: What shall I say? By what name shall I call this monster,
two-formed, which is neither man nor dragon?
Rather, a man without feet, a snake without upper parts —
it can be called a snake-footed man and a man-headed snake.
The man passes out a snake [from below], and the snake has belched out a man,
and the man has no end, the beast no beginning.
So once Cecrops reigned in learned Athens,
so too mother earth brought forth the giants.
This is an image of the crafty; but it points to one who lacks religion
and cares only for earthly things.
Seated on a royal throne, a most beautiful harlot
wears a robe distinguished by the honour of purple,
and to all she offers drink from a full mixing bowl,
while around her a drunken crowd lies sprawling.
So they represent Babylon, which with an enticing appearance
and feigned religion captures foolish nations.

4.motto: Not to you, but to religion.

reading: A slow little ass was carrying the image of Isis,
bearing the revered mysteries on its bent back.
So everyone who meets it reverently worships the goddess
and offers pious prayers on bended knees.
But the ass believes that such honour is shown
to itself, and swells up, very proud,
until the driver, checking it with the whip, said:
“You are not a god, little ass, but you carry a god.”

5.motto: One must go where the gods call.

reading: At a crossroads there is a heap of stones; above it rises
a truncated image of the god, made down to the breast.
This, then, is the mound of Mercury. Hang up, traveller,
garlands to the god: he shows you the right road.
We are all at a crossroads, and on this path of life
we go astray unless God himself shows the way.
Let Honor stand depicted, clothed in a Tyrian cloak,
and let naked Truth join her right hand with his.
And in the middle let there be chaste Love: around his temples
goes a rose; he is fairer than Dione's Cupid.
These signs make up faith: reverence for Honor
cherishes it, Love nourishes it, and Truth gives birth to it.
This lute, which from the shape of a boat is called the “fisherman's”,
and which the Latin Muse claims as her own,
accept, Duke: may our gift please you at this time,
when you are preparing to enter new alliances with your allies.
It is hard, unless one is skilled, to tune so many strings;
and if a single string (fides) is not well stretched
or breaks (which is easy), all the charm of the shell [the instrument] is lost,
and that surpassing song will be out of tune.
So the Italian princes come together in alliances: when there is concord
there is nothing for you to fear, if love stands firm for you.
But if someone falls away (as we generally see),
all that harmony dissolves into nothing.
When he is silent, the fool differs in nothing from the wise.
His tongue and voice are the informers of his folly.
So let him press his lips together, mark silence with his finger,
and turn himself into Pharian Harpocrates.

9.motto: Plans are not to be divulged.

reading: The monster which Daedalus shut up behind a blind threshold and in dark gloom
in the Cnossian hiding places,
the Roman phalanx carries depicted into battle,
and the standards shine proudly with the half-man bull.
They remind us that the secret plans of leaders ought to stay hidden:
a stratagem once known harms its author.

10.motto: Not to yield even to torture.

reading: The lioness you see sculpted in the citadel of Cecrops
was the mistress of Hermodius (do you not know, stranger?).
So they chose to show the fierce spirit of a manly woman,
in the form of a beast, or because she bore such a name [Leaena, “lioness”].
Because, racked on the cords, she betrayed no one
by her testimony, Iphicrates made her tongueless.

11.motto: The Chimaera is overcome by counsel and courage, that is, the stronger and the deceivers.

reading: Bellerophon (as a brave horseman) was able to overcome the Chimaera
and lay low the monsters of the Lycian land.
So you too, borne on the wings of Pegasus, seek the upper air
and by the counsel of your mind tame proud monsters.
Because the cock, by crowing, gives signs of the approaching dawn
and calls the hands of the maidservants back to new spinning,
he is depicted on sacred towers; [and] the bronze basin [bell], because
it calls the wakeful mind back to the gods above [?].
There is also the lion; but because this guardian sleeps with open eyes,
he is therefore placed before the doors of temples.

13.motto: Νῆφε καὶ μέμνησ' ἀπιστεῖν. ἄρθρα ταῦτα τῶν φρενῶν. (“Be sober and remember to distrust: these are the joints of the mind.”) Live soberly, and do not believe rashly.

reading: “Do not believe, and do not be unsober,” says Epicharmus:
these will be the sinews and limbs of the human mind.
Here is the eyed hand, believing what it sees. Here
is pennyroyal (pulegium), the herb of ancient sobriety,
by showing which Heraclitus calmed the crowd
and soothed it when it was heavy with swelling sedition.

greek.original: Νῆφε καὶ μέμνησ' ἀπιστεῖν. ἄρθρα ταῦτα τῶν φρενῶν.
greek.translation: Be sober and remember to distrust: these are the joints of the mind.

14.motto: Πῆ παρέβην? Τί [?] ἔρεξα? Τί μοι δέον, οὐκ ἐτελέσθη? (“Where did I transgress? What [?] did I do? What that I ought to have done was left undone?”) In what have I exceeded? What have I committed? What have I omitted?

reading: The Samian [Pythagoras], most famous founder of the Italian school,
himself enclosed his teaching in a short verse:
“Where have you gone beyond? What are you doing? What do you leave undone that should be done?” —
urging everyone to render this account to himself.
This he is said to have learned from the flock of flying cranes,
which carry a stone seized in their feet,
so as not to stop and so that evil winds do not sweep them off course.
By this rule the life of men was to be governed.

greek.original: Πῆ παρέβην? Τί [?] ἔρεξα? Τί μοι δέον, οὐκ ἐτελέσθη?
greek.translation: Where did I transgress? What [?] did I do? What that I ought to have done was left undone?

reading: Two-faced Janus, you who know both what is past and what is to come,
and who see mockeries behind you (as also in front),
why do they portray you with so many eyes, so many faces? Is it because
the form teaches that you were a circumspect man?
The owl serves as the emblem of Cecropian Athens,
the owl, among birds the bird of sound counsel.
Deservedly she is consecrated to the service of arms-bearing Minerva,
in the place which the chattering crow had formerly given up.
All bid us to make haste quickly and to delay:
not too headlong, nor with too long a delay.
Let this be shown to you by the dart joined to the remora:
the fish is slow, while darts sent from the hand fly.
For a long time I have pursued you wherever you fled; but now
at last you are here, caught in our nets.
No longer will you be able to elude our strength:
we have gripped the eel in a fig leaf.
This is the true image of unwed Pallas; and this is her
dragon, which stands at the feet of its mistress.
Why is this animal the goddess's companion? To it has been given
the guarding of things; so it keeps the groves and sacred temples.
Unwed girls must be protected with ever-wakeful
care: love sets snares everywhere.
This temple is held in common by both, father Bacchus and Pallas,
each a true offspring of Jupiter:
she released his head, he his thigh; to her the use of the olive
is owed, but he first discovered unmixed wine.
They are joined deservedly; and if any abstainer hates
wine, he will feel no help from the goddess.
Why do you trouble me, branches? I am the tree of Pallas:
take the grapes away from here. The virgin flees from Bromius.
Father Bacchus, who has known you with mortal eye,
and who has carved your limbs with skilled hand?
Praxiteles, who saw me carrying off the Cnossian maid [Ariadne],
and portrayed me as I was at that time.
Why are you young, and why does your beard still bloom
with tender down, though you could surpass [in years] the old man of Pylos [Nestor]?
If you learn sometimes to spare my gifts,
you too will always be younger and strong of breast.
Neither drums in your hands nor horns on your head are lacking.
Whom (unless madmen) do such signs befit?
This I teach: whoever has abused our gift puts on
horns, and in his madness shakes soft sistra.
What does that almost fiery colour of your limbs mean? (may the omen
be absent) are you yourself burned on human hearths?
When my father drew me from Semele's womb
with the fire-spewing thunderbolt, he plunged me, smeared with ash, into the waters.
Hence he is wise who dilutes us well with flowing water,
who does not scorch his liver with burning fire.
But now teach me how you wish to be mixed, and by what
law a sane man may take you safely?
Let him add a quarter of water, whoever wishes to drink
a cup of Falernian: in this way cups are pleasant to take [?].
Stay within [two] heminae: for whoever strives to go
further is merry, but soon, drunk, he raves.
This is too hard a thing. Throats are eager [lit. “hanging”], and you
flow sweetly. Alas, no good things come easily.
The fathers [senators] gave Fabius a crown of grass
because by delay he had broken the Carthaginians and Hannibal.
The lark hides her nest for herself in bent grass;
so, it is commonly said, she keeps her chicks warm.
[The grass] is sacred to Saturn and Mars; by eating it Glaucus,
son of Polybus, is believed to have become a god.
By these knots [of grass] protection and safety are rightly signified;
and this finger-grass is green, which has so many [properties] [?].

24.motto: One must harm no one by word or deed.

reading: Nemesis follows and keeps watch on the footsteps of men,
and holds in her hand a cubit [measuring rod] and a hard bridle,
so that you do nothing wrongly and speak no wicked words,
and she bids that measure be present in all things.

25.motto: At last, at last justice prevails.

reading: The shield of Aeacus' descendant [Achilles], drenched with Hector's blood,
which the unjust assembly of the Greeks gave to the Ithacan [Ulysses],
the more just Neptune seized when it was cast into the sea
in the shipwreck, so that it might reach its own master.
For the wave carried it to the shore-side mound of Ajax;
it roars and beats on the tomb with such a voice:
“You have won, son of Telamon, you are more worthy of the arms.”
It is right for partiality to yield to justice.
After the bitter plague of his country,
by killing Cicero, had destroyed Roman eloquence,
he mounted a chariot as victor and yoked lions,
and forced their necks to bear the hard yoke:
Antony wished to show that the great-hearted had yielded to his arms,
meaning the leaders by this figure.
The stork, renowned for its piety, in its nest high in the air
warms its unfledged chicks, its dear pledges,
and expects such gifts to be returned to it in turn
whenever, grown old, the mother will need this help.
Nor does the pious offspring deceive the hope, but carries on its shoulders
the weary bodies of the parents and supplies them food with its beak.
On tombs, on one side of a marble column stands
a jug; on the other a hand-basin can be seen.
This form reminds us that justice was administered without filth
and that the deceased had clean hands.

29.motto: The good have nothing to fear from the rich.

reading: Joined to me by a common wall, Marius, and also
Subbardus, well-known names of our forum,
are building, well provided with money, and even go out of their way
to block, alas, our light on every side.
Wretched me, whom, like Phineus, two Harpies
drag about, to drive me out of my own home —
unless our integrity and our mind that seeks what is honourable
are Zetes against them, are Calais against them.
What cause moves you, Saturnian bird [the eagle],
to sit high upon the tomb of great Aristomenes?
This I proclaim: as much as I excel in strength among birds,
so much does Aristomenes among the demigods.
Let timid doves sit on the tombs of the timid;
we eagles give kindly signs to the fearless.
Sad fortune must be borne by man by enduring it,
and too happy fortune has often had to be feared.
“Bear and forbear,” Epictetus used to say: one must
endure much and keep one's hands from what is forbidden.
So the bull, tied by the right knee, bears the command
of its driver; so it holds itself back from the pregnant [cows].

32.motto: On one who does not know how to flatter.

reading: Do you wish to know why the Thessalian land so often changes
masters and seems to seek to have various rulers?
It does not know how to flatter or to press caresses on anyone,
a custom which every royal court of a prince has;
but like a well-bred horse it throws from its back any
groom who does not know how to manage it.
Yet the master is not permitted to rage; the only vengeance
is to order the wild one to bear a harsher bit.

33.motto: One must hold out against pressure.

reading: The palm strives against the weight and rises into an arch:
the more it is pressed, the higher it lifts the load.
And it bears fragrant fruits, sweet dainties,
which are given the first honour among the courses.
Go, boy, and climbing along the branches gather them: whoever is
constant of mind will win worthy rewards.

34.motto: I carry all my things with me.

reading: The poor Hun, most wretched dweller by the Scythian sea,
his limbs livid, burnt by perpetual frost,
who knows neither the riches of Ceres nor the gifts of Lyaeus,
and yet always has costly coverings:
for skins of mice wrap him tightly on every side.
Only his eyes are open; all the rest he keeps covered.
So he does not fear the thief, so he scorns winds and rains,
safe among men, safe among the gods.
Crows have an amazing concord of life among themselves,
and an inviolate mutual faith remains among them.
Hence sceptres bear these birds: because all
leaders stand and fall by the consent of the people.
If you remove it from their midst, headlong discord
flies in and drags royal doom along with it.
When Rome was preparing leaders for civil war
and the land of Mars was falling by its own strength,
it was the custom, when troops came together on the same side,
to give one another joined right hands as gifts.
This is the image of a covenant: Concord has this sign,
so that those whom love joins, the hand may also join.
Among three brothers there was concord,
so great a mutual devotion and a single love,
that, unconquered by human strength, they held wide
kingdoms and were called by one name, Geryon.

38.motto: One can do nothing, two very much.

reading: The son of Laertes, and together with him the son of Tydeus,
the skilled hand of Zenalis has portrayed in this wax.
This one excels in strength, that one is powerful in sharpness of mind,
and yet each needs the help of the other.
When the two come joined together, victory is certain;
a man alone is failed either by mind or by right hand.

39.motto: The most firmly rooted cannot be torn up.

reading: Though father Ocean should stir up all his waves,
and you, barbarian Turk, should drink the whole Danube,
yet you will not burst in by breaking the frontier, while Caesar
Charles gives the peoples the standards of war.
So the sacred oaks stand on firm roots,
though the winds shake their dry leaves.
Your commonwealth is tossed by countless storms,
and only hope of future safety is at hand:
just like a ship in the midst of the sea, which the winds
sweep along, and which is already breaking up in the salt waters.
But if the shining stars, the brothers of Helen, appear,
good hope restores lost courage.
What goddess is this, looking up at the stars with so joyful a face?
By whose brushes was this image rendered?
The hands of Elpidius made it. I am she who is called
Good Hope, who offers the wretched ready help.
Why is your cloak green? Because under my guidance all things bloom.
Why do you carry in your hands the broken arrows of death?
Because the living should hope; for the buried I cut hope off.
Why do you sit idly on the lid of a little jar?
I alone stayed at home when evils flew off in all directions,
as the revered muse of the old man of Ascra [Hesiod] taught.
What bird is that beside you? The crow, most faithful of omen-birds:
when it cannot say “it is well”, it says “it will be”.
Who are your companions? Good Outcome and headlong Cupid.
Who go before? They are called the empty dreams of the waking.
Who stands joined to you? Rhamnusia [Nemesis], avenger of crimes,
that is, so that you may hope for nothing but what is permitted.
At the new year a client offered me the snout of a bristly pig,
and said: “Take this gift for your belly.”
It always moves forward and never looks back
when, greedy, it roots up the grass with its bent snout.
Men have the same concern: that hope should not slip and fall
back, and that what is further should be better.

43.motto: The unlawful is not to be hoped for.

reading: Hope and Nemesis are present together at our altars,
that is, so that you may hope for nothing but what is permitted.
If in the master's house the wife commits adultery,
the porphyrion loses heart and dies of grief.
The cause is hidden in the secrets of nature. Let this bird
be a sure sign of pure chastity.

45.motto: On a victory won by guile.

reading: I, Virtue, bathe the tomb of Ajax with tears,
alas, wretched, having torn my whitening hair.
This, of course, was still left: that by a Greek judge
I should be defeated, and that guile should prevail over the better cause.
The little lizard, the stellio, its body starred with dark
spots, which haunts hiding places and hollow tombs,
when depicted carries the symbols of envy and wicked guile;
alas, all too well known to jealous wives.
For anyone's face is covered with ugly freckles
who drinks wine in which a stellio has been steeped.
Hence a frequent revenge: the mistress is tricked with the wine,
and her lover abandons her once the flower of her beauty is lost.
A fattened decoy duck, blue in its plumage,
and accustomed to go back and forth to its masters,
seeing flocks of its own kind flying through the air,
quacks, and joins their flock,
until it leads the unwary under the spread nets.
The captives make an uproar, but she herself, knowing, is silent.
The treacherous bird pollutes itself with kindred blood,
obliging to others, deadly to its own.
They say that on the tomb of Archilochus there are wasps carved in marble,
sure seals of an evil tongue.
A band of robbers and thieves, Scaeva, goes through the city
as your retinue, and a cohort girt with dreadful swords.
And so, spendthrift, you consider yourself generous of spirit,
because your pot attracts many villains.
Behold a new Actaeon, who, after he had put on horns,
gave himself as prey to his own dogs.
Always gaping, always the thin air on which it feeds
the chameleon breathes in and out,
and changes its appearance and takes on various colours,
except red or white.
So too the flatterer feeds on the breeze of popular favour,
and, gaping, devours everything,
and imitates only the black ways of the prince,
knowing nothing of the white and modest.

51.motto: To one who has once squandered his own, others' goods should not be entrusted.

reading: Why do you build your nest in the bosom of the Colchian woman? Alas,
ignorant bird, why do you entrust your chicks so badly?
Medea, a dreadful mother, most cruel, destroyed
her own children, and do you hope that she will spare yours?
Headlong he is swept along, and in vain he pulls at the reins,
the driver carried by a horse with an unbridled mouth.
You would not easily trust one whom no reason governs
and who is rashly led by his own will.
The shield bears the painted face of a raging lion
and has a verse written on its upper rim:
“This is the terror of men”; its owner, the son of Atreus,
great-hearted Agamemnon, bore such devices.
You see Phaethon, driver of his father's chariot,
who dared to steer the fire-breathing horses of the Sun.
After he had scattered the greatest fires over the earth,
the wretch fell from the axle he had rashly mounted.
So too most kings, raised to the stars by the wheels of Fortune,
whom youthful ambition drives,
after great ruin of the human race and their own,
at last pay the penalty for all their crimes.

55.motto: On those who dare anything beyond their strength.

reading: While he sleeps, while he refreshes his body with sweet sleep
under a spruce, and holds his club and his other weapons,
the band of Pygmies thinks it can put Alcides
to death, poorly aware of its own strength.
Awakened, he crushes the enemy like fleas,
and drives them along wrapped in the skin of the savage lion.
You wash an Ethiopian: why in vain? Ah, stop. The darkness
of black night no one can light up.
Why do many call country folk, the rustic kind,
cuckoos, and what cause has been given for it?
In early spring the cuckoo (coccyx) sings; whoever by that time
has not finished [the work on] his vines is rightly marked as idle.
It lays its eggs in others' nests, like the man
whose marriage bed his wife betrays by adultery.
That he took his name from the bird, the daughter of Minyas (Meneis) [the bat]:
so the authors report of Chaerephon the Socratic.
The man had a swarthy face and a squeaky little voice: with such
a mark could this man be branded.
She who flies only at evening, who is weak of sight,
who, though she bears wings, has all else of a mouse,
is applied to different things. First she signifies
men of bad name, who lurk and fear judgment.
Next, philosophers too, who, while they seek heavenly things,
grow dim of eye and see only what is false.
Lastly, the crafty too, who, secretly following both [sides],
win trust with neither side.
The ancients called the lion's tail the alcaea:
spurred by it, he conceives heavy wrath.
When the yellow bile rises, and pain grows raw
with black gall, it rouses untamed fury.

61.motto: On one who prepares harm for himself.

reading: I, the goat, not of my own will, now suckle a wolf at my udder,
because the ill-provident care of the shepherd orders it.
As soon as he has grown, after my udder he will feed on me.
Wickedness is not softened by any kindness.
You wonder that in our song you are called Otus,
since you have from your forefathers the ancient name Otho.
It is an eared bird, and has feathers like an owl's,
and the skilful fowler takes the bird while it dances.
Hence we call fools, and those easy to catch, “oti”;
you too, have this name that suits you.

63.motto: Forgetfulness is the mother of poverty.

reading: When the hungry lynx (lupus cervarius) is chewing its food
and from hunger devours a captured fawn,
if by chance it looks elsewhere or turns its eyes,
forgetting the present food it holds in its claw,
it seeks uncertain prey (so great is its forgetfulness).
He who foolishly neglected his own seeks what belongs to others.
Behold a statue of a statue, marble carved out of marble:
insolent Niobe, who dared to compare herself with the gods.
Pride is a woman's vice, and it betrays a hardness
of face and feeling such as is in stone.
A woman down to the groin, girt below with the barking
whelps of monsters: such was two-formed Scylla.
Avarice, boldness, rapine are held to be the monsters.
But Scylla is the one in whose face there is no shame.
Because your beauty [pleased] you too much, Narcissus [?],
it has been turned into a flower and the plant of well-known numbness (νάρκη).
Self-love is the withering and ruin of talent: it
ruins and has ruined many learned men,
who, casting aside the method of the ancients, seek new doctrines
and hand down nothing but their own fantasies.
Why, chattering Procne, do you break my morning sleep,
and sing, Daulian, with your noisy mouth?
Tereus deserved to be a hoopoe, he who preferred to prune with the sword
rather than to root out the immoderate tongue.
A squalid woman chewing the flesh of vipers,
whose eyes ache and who eats her own heart,
whom leanness and pallor possess, and who carries thorny
darts in her hand: thus is Envy depicted.
Goat-footed Faunus, his temples wreathed with rocket (eruca),
displays the sure symbols of immoderate Venus.
Rocket is lustful, the he-goat is the betrayer of lust,
and satyrs are always wont to love nymphs.
On airy cliffs and on the edge of a high rock
the bitter fig tree bears ungentle fruits,
which ravens eat, which the shameless crow devours,
and which have nothing of use for man.
So parasites and harlots enjoy the riches of fools,
and they help the just with no benefit.

71.subheading: Διαλογιστικῶς (“In the form of a dialogue”).

reading: What tomb is this? Whose urn? It is that of Lais of Ephyra.
Ah, did not
Fate (Parca) blush to destroy such beauty?
There was no beauty then: age had already plucked it,
and the old woman had already prudently dedicated her mirror to Venus.
What does the carved ram mean, which a lioness
holds, seized with her claws by its hind part?
That she too held her captured lovers in the same way:
the ram is the husband of the flock; the lover is held by the haunch (clunis).

greek.translation: In the form of a dialogue.

reading: A fisherman, clothed in the covering of a shaggy goat,
having added two horns to his head,
standing at the very edge of the shore, deceives the amorous sargus,
which desire for the snub-nosed flock drives into the snares.
The goat represents the harlot; the sargus becomes like the lover,
who, wretched, perishes, caught by obscene love.
So great is said to have been the power of Circe, child of the Sun,
that she turned many men into strange monsters.
Witness Picus, tamer of horses, then two-formed Scylla,
and the [companions] of the Ithacan, swine after they had drunk the wine.
Circe, with a famous name, signifies the harlot,
and [shows] that whoever loves loses the reason of his mind.
Adonis, pierced in the groin by the savage tusk, Cypris
laid lifeless in the leaves of lettuce.
Hence lettuce resists the genital field as much
as lustful rocket can barely stimulate it.
So that dire love may not conquer you, and that no woman
may tear your mind apart with magic arts,
let the Bacchic bird, the wagtail, be ready for you,
which you are to place four-rayed in the round of a wheel,
so that it may form a cross with beak, tail and both wings:
such an amulet will be [proof] against every spell.
By this sign of Venus, it is said, Pagasaean Jason
could not be harmed by the wiles of the Phasis [of Colchis].
The white mouse is believed to signify luxury
and softness, but the reason is not quite clear to me.
Is it because its nature is lustful and its desire great?
Or because it adorns Roman wives with its fur?
Many call the Sarmatian mouse the sable (zibellus),
and the Arabian musk is famous for its sweet ointment.
The Essene sits idle in a bushel measure (modius), a watcher of the stars,
and beneath it hides a torch lit with fire.
Sloth under the guise of righteousness, veiled by a cowl,
benefits neither itself nor others.
Let whoever is idle go away. For to sit down on the choenix [a grain measure]
the holy teachings of the old man of Samos [Pythagoras] forbid us.
Rise, then, and accustom your hands to hard labour,
so that tomorrow's hour may give you your measured food.

79.motto: On those who easily fall away from virtue.

reading: As the little slug (limax), the remora, scorning the force of the wind
and of the oars (remorum), alone can stop a ship,
so some men, borne by talent and virtue towards the stars,
are held back in mid-course by a trifling cause:
such as an anxious lawsuit, or the passion for harlots
which draws young men away from excellent studies.
An ancient tale held that the starry heron portrays an idle slave,
both his pursuits and his manners.
It invented that the servant Asterias took the shape of the bird:
let the credit for this rest with the historians.
It is like a degenerate falcon which [?] in the air,
called “ardelio” [a busy idler] by the ancient poets.
Alas, wretched Tantalus stands thirsting in the midst of the waters,
and, hungry, cannot get the fruits close by.
With the name changed, this will be said of you, miser,
who, as though you did not have it, do not enjoy what you have.
Septitius, the richest among all the people,
an old man than whom no one holds wider fields,
cheating both his genius and the tables laid ready,
eats nothing but beets and hard turnips.
To whom shall I compare him, whom abundance makes poor?
To an ass? So it is: he is just like one.
For the ass carries costly delicacies on its back,
and feeds itself, poor beast, on bramble or hard sedge.
The empty court is said to bind the palace clients it rears
with golden fetters [?].
The ibis, which with its beak (as with a clyster) flushes out its belly,
known on the banks of the Nile,
has passed into a term of abuse: by it Publius Naso [Ovid] calls
his enemy, and Battiades [Callimachus] his.

85.motto: On those who grow rich from public misfortune.

reading: Whoever catches eels, if he sweeps clear
rivers, if he dares to approach unclouded lakes,
will come away empty and waste his labour; so let him stir up much
mud [?], and let the oar trouble the glassy waters:
he will be rich. So a troubled commonwealth is profit to those
who in peace, restricted by the laws, go hungry.

86.motto: On misers, or on those to whom strangers offer a better lot.

reading: Sitting on a dolphin, Arion furrows the blue waters,
and with this sound soothes its ears and bridles its mouth.
The mind of wild creatures is not so cruel as that of a greedy man:
we who are plundered by men are rescued by fish.
A man is painted with a crane's gullet and swollen belly,
who carries in his hands a gull or a pelican (onocrotalus).
Such was the figure of Dionysius, and such of Apicius,
and of those whom dainty gluttony makes famous.

88.motto: The figure of Ocnus. On those who give to harlots what ought to be turned to good uses.

reading: Tireless, he never stops plaiting a rope of esparto
and joining the moist strands with skilled hand.
But as much as he, diligent, barely twists in many hours,
the she-ass of the idle belly at once devours.
A woman, an idle animal, seizes the gains amassed
by an easy-going husband, and squanders them on her finery.
Accept the river crabs which we give you:
these gifts suit your ways.
They have watchful eyes, and a numerous row of claws
armed with pincers, and a huge belly is there.
So your stomach sticks out with its fat paunch,
and swift feet, and stings fit for the foot [?],
when you wander through the crossroads and the benches of the table,
and, biting, throw false jibes at others.

90.motto: A small kitchen is not enough for two gluttons.

reading: In small things there is nothing for anyone to gain, and one
thicket does not feed two robins (erithacus).

epigrams.label: Another.
reading: In what is meagre there is no hope of gain, and on one
tree two figpeckers do not sit well together.
The ruler [?] of the larder and gnawer of the master's table,
a mouse, saw oysters gaping at the edges of their lips.
When, putting in his tender whiskers, he bit their deceptive bones [?],
they, touched, suddenly closed their house,
and held the caught thief in a gloomy prison,
he who had given himself into a dark tomb.
It booms with a harsh voice, it has a huge throat, its beak
is like a nose and a many-holed trumpet.
An ugly ranter, addicted to belly and gullet,
the bird truo will signify, when it is painted.
It is an old custom that to professors
some nicknames should be added.
Explaining only easy and open passages,
Curtius is called “Canon”.
He who turns round and round the same thing and repeats too much
is a “Meander”, like Parisius.
Obscure and confused, as Picus was,
he will be called a “Labyrinth”.
Too brief, cutting away much, like Claudius,
he will bear the nickname “Point” (Mucro).
Parpalus, who breaks even columns with his voice,
is called a “truo” by the scholars.
On the contrary, Albius, because he was thin
of voice, was called a “bat”.
But Crassus, maiming the last syllables like a docked creature (colobotes),
is called a “swallow”.
He who, deaf to others, wants to speak alone
is, as in the proverb, a “starling”.
This one lisps, that one is hoarse, this one chatters.
This one hisses like a viper.
That one makes an uproar with his jaws and nostrils.
This one's tongue works like a gimlet.
Another hiccups, and coughs as he hesitates.
Another spatters spittle like a sprinkling maid (psecas).
As many vices as are at work in human affairs,
so many names arise.
The nations worship Pan (that is to say, the nature of things),
a half-goat man and a half-man god.
Down to the groin he is a man, because the virtue implanted in us,
rising in the heart, sits in the lofty citadel of the head.
Below he is a goat, because nature propagates us through the ages
by coupling, as it does birds, scaly creatures, cattle and beasts.
What is common [to us] with other living things, the goat, the betrayer
of lust, [signifies], and he bears the open signs of Venus.
Some have assigned wisdom (sophia) to the heart, others to the brain.
The lower parts are ruled by no measure and no reason.
As Fortune sits on a sphere, so Hermes sits on a cube:
he presides over the arts, she over varied chances.
Against the force of Fortune art was made; but when
fortune is bad, it often needs the help of art.
Learn, then, the good arts, studious youth:
they bring with them the advantages of a sure lot.
Both sons of Jupiter, both tender and beardless,
he whom Latona bore, and he whom Semele bore,
hail, and flourish together in eternal youth,
and by your divine power may it be lasting for me.
You, wash away cares with wine; you, diseases with diet,
so that late old age may come on with slow foot.

97.motto: On the four seasons of the year.

reading: That winter has come, the chaffinch announces.
In early spring the chattering swallow returns to us.
The cuckoo shows that it is waiting for summer.
In autumn alone can figpeckers be seen.
Accept this mixing bowl of Nestor with twin bases,
a work which a heavy mass of silver poured forth.
The studs are of gold; around it stand four handles;
on each one sits a golden dove.
Only long-lived Nestor could lift it.
Teach me, what does the muse of the Maeonian [Homer] mean?
The cup itself is the sky: its colour is silver;
the golden studs are the stars of the sky.
The doves he spoke of are thought to be the Pleiades.
The twin bosses [bases] are the Greater and the Lesser Beast [the Bears].
These things wise Nestor understands through long experience:
the brave wage wars, the shrewd grasp the stars.

99.motto: What is above us is nothing to us.

reading: Prometheus, hanging eternally on the Caucasian rock,
has his liver torn by the talon of the sacred bird.
And he would wish not to have made man; and, hating potters,
he curses the torch lit from the stolen fire.
The hearts of the wise are gnawed by various cares,
those who aspire to know [the secrets] of heaven and the turns of the gods.
Icarus, you who were carried up through the heavens and the air, until
the melted wax sent you headlong into the sea,
now the same wax and burning fire raise you up again,
so that by your example you may teach sure doctrines.
Let the astrologer beware of predicting anything: for
the impostor will fall headlong while he flies above the stars.

101.motto: Those who contemplate lofty things fall.

reading: While the fowler deceives thrushes with lime, larks with a snare,
and with a cast reed transfixes the high-flying crane,
unwary, he struck a dipsas with his foot; avenger
of the wrong, it shoots venom from its mouth.
So dies he who, with bow drawn, looks up at the stars,
careless of the fate that lies before his feet.
See how the unconquered charioteer overcomes the strength of the lion —
Love, a little boy carved on a gem;
how with this hand he holds the whip, with that he guides the reins,
and how great is the beauty in the boy's face.
Dread plague, keep far away: he who is able to conquer such a beast,
will he keep his hands from us?
Do you see how naked Love laughs and gazes calmly [?]?
He has neither torches nor a bow to bend.
But one of his hands holds flowers, the other a fish,
to show, of course, that he gives laws to the land and to the sea.
The winged god has broken the winged thunderbolt, with fire
showing that love is a fire stronger than fire.

105.motto: On a scholar captured by Love.

reading: Immersed in his studies, learned in pleading and in law,
and the greatest of petition-writers (libellio),
he loves Helianira more than ever the Thracian
prince [Tereus] loved his concubine, [his wife's] sister.
Why, Cypris, did you overcome Pallas before another judge?
Is it not enough to win beneath Ida?

106.motto: Αντέρως, id amor virtutis (“Anteros, that is, the love of virtue”).
106.subheading: Διαλογιστικῶς (“In the form of a dialogue”).

reading: Tell me, where are your curved bows? Where are the darts, Cupid,
with which [?] you are wont to pierce the tender hearts of young men?
Where is the grim torch? Where are the wings? Why does your hand
carry three garlands? Why do your temples wear another, girt around?
“I have nothing (stranger) to do with common Cypris,
nor has any form of pleasure carried me away;
but I kindle in the pure minds of men the fires
of learning, and I draw souls to the high stars.
From Virtue herself I weave four garlands,
and the one of them that belongs to Wisdom covers [?] my temples first.”

greek.translation: In the form of a dialogue.

107.motto: Αντέρως (“Anteros”), the Love of virtue, overcoming the other Cupid.

reading: Nemesis has portrayed a winged one, hostile to winged Love,
and so tames bow with bow, and fires with fire,
so that he may suffer what he has done to others. But this boy, once
fearlessly carrying his darts, now weeps in misery.
He spits three times deep into his bosom: (a wondrous thing) fire
is burned by fire, Love hates the furies of Love.
His mother left far away, the Lydian child had wandered off
a little; but you, dreadful bees, seized him.
He had come to you thinking you were gentle winged creatures,
when not even the savage viper would have been so pitiless.
Ah, you give stings in return for the sweet gift of honey!
O pain! Alas, without you no pleasure is given.
While he was gathering honey from the hives, a wicked bee stung
thievish Love, and left its stings in the tips
of his fingers; but the boy groans in distress at his swollen fingertip,
and, wandering about, stamps the ground; and to Venus his pain
he shows, and complains bitterly that a little bee, a small
animal, can itself inflict such harmful wounds.
Venus, laughing, said to him: “You too imitate this
creature, son: you, being small, inflict so many harmful wounds.”
What love is, many poets once sang,
who tell of his deeds under various names.
They agree on this: that he lacks clothing, that he is small of body,
carrying darts and wings, he has no eyes.
These are the god's face and appearance. But if it is permitted to speak
against such great poets, I think that falsehood lies beneath.
For why does he go naked? As if the god lacked cloaks,
he who possesses all the riches of the conquered world.
Or how, I ask, could he, naked, escape the snows and the Alpine
north wind, and the meadows bound with frost?
If he is a boy, do you call a boy one who is older than Nestor?
Or do you not know the learned songs of the old man of Ascra [Hesiod]?
A boy is inconstant, but this one is stubborn: the hearts he has
once entered he can never leave of his own accord.
He carries quivers and darts: why this useless weight?
Can an infant bend a hard bow?
Or why does he have wings, if he cannot carry them into the upper air,
not knowing how to aim his darts at the livers of birds?
He creeps on the ground and always wounds the mortal hearts
of men, and, like stone, he never moves his wings from there.
If he is blind and wears a band, of what use to a blind man
is a ribbon? Does he see the less for it?
And who would believe him to be an archer, who is deprived of sight?
This one sends sure darts, but the blind man's are vain.
He is fiery, they say, and turns flames about in the breast.
Why then, come, is he still alive? Flame devours all things.
And moreover, why is he not extinguished in the swelling waves,
whenever he enters the soft hearts of the Naiads?
But you, so as not to be caught by such great errors, listen:
what true Love is, our verses will tell.
He is pleasant labour in wanton leisure; his
sign is a pomegranate (punica glans) on a black shield.
Having long since left your country and forgotten your own,
whom either blood or love has given you,
you live in Rome, and no thought of returning home comes to you:
only the honour of the eternal city captivates you.
So the band of the Ithacan, sent ahead, through the sweetness of the lotus
had abandoned both their country and their leader.
Birds without wings, and girls without legs,
and fish without a beak, who nevertheless sing with their mouths:
who would think that such exist? Nature has refused to join these things,
but the Sirens teach that it could have been done.
Unlawful is the woman who ends in a black fish,
because lust brings with it a great many monsters.
By appearance, by words, by brightness of mind, men are drawn
by Parthenope, Ligia and Leucosia.
The Muses pluck their feathers, and Ulysses mocks them.
That is, the learned have nothing to do with a harlot.

113.motto: An old man in love with a girl.

reading: When Sophocles (though of advanced age) drew the girl
Archippe, who lived by her earnings, to his desires,
and enticed her with money, the mad youth took it badly
out of jealousy, and branded both with such a verse:
“As the owl on tombs, as the horned owl above corpses,
so sits our girl beside Sophocles.”
Dark colour is the sign of grief: we all use
this dress when we make offerings at tombs.
But the white stole [is the sign] of a sincere spirit and a pure mind.
Hence linen sindon is pleasing to holy men.
Green teaches us to hope. Hope is said to be
“in the green” whenever, unfulfilled, it falls back [?].
Yellow is the colour for the passionate; it suits lovers too,
and harlots, and those whose hope was sure.
But let a red cloak adorn armed horsemen,
and let shame show that boys have blushed.
Blue [suits] sailors, and seers who seek heavenly things,
thunderstruck by excessive religion.
Cheap are the grey cloaks of undyed wool,
such as the wooden-footed [friars] usually have for coverings.
He whom huge cares torment, or the jealousy of love,
is thought to be not badly clothed in a tawny garment.
Whoever is content with his lot, let him wear violet,
and [he] who bears the vexations of Fortune with an even mind.
As nature is varied in producing colours,
so one thing [pleases] some, another others: but to each his own are pleasing.
The caduceus, with intertwined snakes and twin wings,
stands upright between the horns of Amalthea.
Thus it shows that men powerful in mind and skilled in speaking
are blessed by a great abundance of goods.
After, defeated by Caesar's soldiers, he saw
Pharsalia flowing with civil blood,
on the point of driving the sword into his dying breast,
Brutus uttered these words with bold mouth:
“Unhappy Virtue, provident only in words,
why in deeds do you follow Fortune as your mistress?”

117.motto: Poverty hinders the highest talents from advancing.

reading: My right hand holds a stone, the other supports wings.
As the feather raises me, so the heavy burden sinks me.
By my talent I could fly through the heights above,
if envious poverty did not weigh me down.

118.subheading: Διαλογιστικῶς (“In the form of a dialogue”).

reading: This is the work of Lysippus, whose country is Sicyon. Who are you?
The moment of seized time, which subdues all things.
Why do you stand on wings? I am always whirling. Why do you keep
winged sandals on your feet? The light breeze carries me everywhere.
Tell me, why is there a thin razor in your right hand? This sign
teaches that I am sharper than any blade.
Why is there hair on your forehead? So that I may be seized as I come. But, you there,
tell me, why is the back of your head bald?
So that, if anyone once lets me, wing-footed, go,
I may not afterwards be caught by grasping my hair.
With such art the craftsman made us for your sake, stranger,
and so that I may warn everyone, an open portico holds me.

greek.translation: In the form of a dialogue.

reading: Seeing troops fleeing with their column scattered,
“Who is blowing my horns now?” says Faunus.

120.motto: On those who praise what is not praiseworthy.

reading: The huge troops of the Galatians, with his half-armed soldiers,
trembling Antiochus had routed beyond hope,
when the savage force of the Lucanian oxen [elephants], the fury of the trunk,
first seized the enemy horses.
So, setting up a trophy, he painted it with the image of an elephant,
and moreover said to his comrades: “We would have perished,
had not that most loathsome beast, the elephant (barrus), saved us.”
As it is pleasing to have won, so it is shameful to have won [thus].
A gourd is said to have grown up beside a lofty pine
and to have run riot with great foliage.
When it had embraced the branches and gone beyond the very top,
it believed itself superior to the other trees.
To it the pine said: “This glory is too brief, for
the winter will soon come that will cruelly destroy you.”
While they rushed with savage weapons to wound each other,
the lioness fierce with claw, the boar fearsome with tusk,
the vulture runs up to watch, and lies in wait for a meal:
the glory of the victor will be his prey.

123.motto: One must begin under good auspices.

reading: A thing begun under bad auspices cannot turn out well.
What is done with a happy omen brings benefit.
Whatever you are doing, if a weasel meets you, leave it off:
this wicked creature bears the signs of ill fortune.
This, of course, was lacking: that after so many evils at last
locusts should snatch from our fields whatever was in them.
We saw countless hosts advancing with the east wind as their leader,
such as were not Attila's, nor the camps of Xerxes.
They have consumed the hay, the millet, all the spelt;
and hope too is in a narrow strait, unless vows remain.
A greedy kite, whom nausea from too much food had racked,
said: “Woe is me, mother, my entrails are flowing from my mouth.”
But she: “Why do you weep? Why should you believe these are your entrails,
you who, living by plunder, vomit only what belongs to others?”
Three girls of equal age were once playing
at lots: which should go first to the Stygian waters.
But she to whom the die had fallen badly when the knucklebone was thrown
was laughing, blind to her own lot,
when suddenly, struck on the head by a collapsing roof, she died,
and paid the debt of fate owed for her bold jest.
In adversity a bad lot is not mistaken; but in
fortunate things there is no room for prayers or for the hand.
After Jupiter cast Ate down from the ethereal seats,
alas, how that evil bane torments men!
She flies off, swift of foot and with rapid wings,
and allows nothing to remain untouched by misfortunes.
So the Litae, the offspring of Jupiter, accompany her as she goes,
to mend whatever evil she has done.
But because they are slow-footed, half-blind and weary with age,
they restore nothing except afterwards, after a long time.

128.motto: From hard things, an everlasting name.

reading: A sparrow had entrusted its young to the branches of a plane tree,
and well, had they not been seen by a savage dragon.
It swallowed all the chicks and the wretched mother,
turned to stone, and worthy to die such a death.
These, unless Calchas lies, are the monuments of a long
labour, whose fame is everlasting.

129.motto: Immortality is gained through the study of letters.

reading: Neptune's trumpeter, whose lower part shows a sea-monster,
while his face shows him to be a god of the sea,
Triton is enclosed in the middle of a serpent's ring,
which holds its tail with its mouth thrust into it.
Fame attends men distinguished in spirit, and glorious deeds,
and commands that they be read throughout the world.

130.motto: The tomb of Giovanni Galeazzo Visconti, first Duke of Milan.

reading: For a tomb set up Italy, set up arms and leaders,
and the sea that roars as far as its twin gulfs.
Add to these barbarism vainly trying to break in,
and hands bought for pay for savage wars.
Let the serpent-bearer, standing on the very top, say:
“Who has set me, who am great, on top of small things?”
While Thrasybulus frees his country with just arms,
and while he bids everyone lay aside their feuds,
the whole order [of citizens], in concord, as a great reward,
gave him a wreath of Pallas' foliage to wear.
Bind your hair, Thrasybulus; bear this honour alone:
in the great city no one is your rival.

132.motto: The immortal name of the valiant.

reading: You see the tomb of Aeacus' descendant [Achilles] on the Rhoetean shore,
which white Thetis often visits on foot.
This stone is always covered with green amaranth,
because the hero's honour will never die.
Here is the wall of the Greeks, the death of great Hector. He owes
no more to the Maeonian [Homer] than the Maeonian owes to him.
A golden brooch fastened the Cecropian garments,
to which a cicada was joined, clinging fast with its tooth.
The shoe beneath which, in Arcadian fashion, there was a little moon,
is worn, red (mullea), by the fathers, sons of Romulus,
because they claimed to be natives of the soil: these signs were borne
by men famous for ancient nobility.
Eloquence surpasses the praises of unconquered strength:
it unties the sayings and empty snares of the Sophists.
No fury or rage is more powerful than virtue.
Wealth yields to the wise man because of his unbroken course.
He scorns avarice, and takes no joy in plunder or usury.
He conquers effeminate deeds and strips them of their insignia.
He cleans away filth and adds cultivation to minds.
He hates unlawful unions and drives away the guilty.
Barbarism and impious savagery at last pay the penalty.
The virtue of one man scatters gathered enemies.
He brings into his country many goods from foreign shores.
He flies through the learned mouths of men and never perishes.
Bastards, may you always celebrate the honours of Hercules:
for he was the chief of your order.
Nor could he become a god before, as an infant, he had sucked
the milk which Juno, unaware of the deceit, gave him.
As the falcon, flying on high, cleaves the thin air,
as the jackdaw, the goose and the duck feed on the ground,
so mighty Pindar climbs above the highest heaven,
so Bacchylides knows only how to creep along the ground.
In that you have stained an excellent beginning with a shameful end,
and turned your service into harm,
you have done what the goat does when she strikes the pail
of her milk and with her hoof spills out her own riches.
The degenerate kite accompanies the high-flying harpa
and often gets a part of the prey that falls.
The sargus follows the red mullet (mullus), and greedily devours with its mouth
the food the mullet has spurned and passed over.
So Oenocrates acts towards me: but the deserted curia of the students
uses this blear-eyed man as though he were an eye.

139.motto: Albutius to Alciato, advising him to withdraw from the Italian troubles and to teach in France.

reading: The tree that gave these fruits, a newcomer to our sky,
came formerly from the eastern regions of Persia.
By transplanting it was made better: once harmful
in its native land, here it bears sweet fruits for us.
It bears a leaf like a tongue, it bears fruits most like a heart.
Alciato, learn from this how to spend your life.
Far from your country you will be held at a higher price:
you are very wise in heart, and no less strong in speech.

140.motto: The prince caring for the safety of his subjects.

reading: Whenever the Titan-born brothers [the winds] throw the seas into turmoil,
then the cast anchor helps the wretched sailors.
The dolphin, devoted to men, embraces it, so that
it may be fixed more safely in the depths of the sea-bed.
How fitting it is for mindful kings to bear this device,
[remembering] that they are to their people what the anchor is to sailors!

141.motto: On the senate of a good prince.

reading: Figures cut off at the hands sit here
before the altars of the gods; the first of them is deprived of sight.
These signs of the highest power and of the holy senate
were devised by the men of Thebes.
Why do they sit? Because it befits judges to be grave
with a calm mind, and not to waver with a light spirit.
Why are they without hands? So that they may take no gifts, nor let
themselves be swayed by promises or presents.
But the prince is blind, because, by his ears alone, without
partiality, he steadfastly carries out the decrees of the senate.

142.motto: What Christ does not take, the treasury seizes.

reading: The tight hand of a greedy prince squeezes out
the wet sponges which it had soaked before.
He raises thieves to the top, and then punishes them,
so as to turn into his own treasury what was ill gotten.

143.motto: The wealth of the tyrant is the poverty of the subjects.

reading: What the spleen is in the human body, that in the state,
Caesar had said, is his treasury.
When the spleen is enlarged, the other limbs of the body waste away.
When the treasury is enlarged, it betrays the poverty of the citizens.
It is said that the sons of heroes and great Achilles
were educated by Chiron in his stables.
A half-beast teacher, a half-man centaur,
is what anyone who sits beside kings should be.
He is a beast when he outrages allies, when he tramples enemies;
and he is a man when he pretends to the people to be devout.
That the king of the wasps will never fix a sting,
and that he will be twice as large in body as the others,
signifies a clement rule and a moderate reign,
and holy laws entrusted to good judges.
The Epidaurian son of Phoebus [Aesculapius] sits on raised altars,
a gentle god, and is hidden in a huge serpent.
The sick run to him and pray that the saviour may come:
he nods assent and makes their prayers come true.
On the death of Caesar, as if liberty had been recovered,
this coin was struck by the leaders, the Bruti.
On it are, first, little daggers, above which stands a cap,
such as slaves receive when they are set free.
Weep now more than usual for the troubles of human life,
Heraclitus: it swarms with more evils.
You, in turn (if ever before), raise a guffaw,
Democritus: it has become more laughable.
Meanwhile, seeing these things, I ponder at last to what end
I should weep with you, or how I should jest with you from the spleen.

149.motto: Safety must sometimes be bought with money.

reading: Both slow of foot and hanging down with a swollen belly,
the beaver nevertheless escapes ambushes by this art:
he himself bites off his medicinal genitals
and throws them away, knowing that he is hunted for them.
From his example you will learn not to spare your possessions,
and, to ransom your life, to give money to your enemies.

150.motto: One must not wrestle with ghosts.

reading: Hector, dying from the thrust of the spear of Aeacus' descendant,
he who had so often before conquered his enemies,
could not hold back his voice as they insulted him,
while they prepared the bonds for the chariot and his feet:
“Tear me apart as you please: so even timid hares
pluck the beard of a lion deprived of light.”
Death was wandering, joined with Cupid as her companion. With her
Death carried quivers, little Love his darts.
They turned aside to lodge together, and together slept for one night:
Love is blind, and Death was blind at that time.
For each, ill-providing, took the other's darts:
Death the golden ones, the boy holds the darts of bone.
Hence an old man who ought by now to be bound for Acheron,
behold, is in love, and prepares flowery garlands for his head.
But I, because Love struck me with the exchanged bow,
am failing: the fates lay their hand on me too.
Spare me, boy; Death, holding the victorious standards, spare me.
Make me love; make the old man go down to Acheron.

152.motto: On a beautiful girl snatched away by fate before her time.

reading: Why, Death, have you dared to carry off the boy Love by guile?
So that he might throw your darts while he thinks them his own.
The boy who with his beauty attracted and tormented tender girls,
most beautiful, and famous in the whole city,
died before his day, to be wept for by no one more (Arestius)
than by you, to whom he was joined by chaste love.
So you build him a tomb, a monument of so great a grief,
and strike the stars with plaintive cries:
“Do you go without me, beloved? Shall we no longer go together?
Will you not spend pleasant leisure with me in our studies?
But earth will cover you, but the face of the Gorgon
and the dolphins will give mournful signs of your fate.”
A square stone, a most solid block, is sunk in the ground;
above it stands a curly-haired image, down to the breast,
and declares that it yields to no one. Such
is Terminus, the single goal that drives men.
The day is immovable, and times are fixed beforehand by the fates,
and the last things pass judgment on the first.
On this side the Trojans drag Patroclus off in false armour;
on that side his comrades and the whole Pelasgian crowd prevent them.
Hector gets the spoils, the Greeks the corpse.
This little fable is acted out when a wealthy man dies.
A very great quarrel arises, but at last the heir comes to terms,
and leaves something to the ravens and vultures.
An elm, withered with age and stripped of its leaves,
a vine, shady with green foliage, has embraced.
It acknowledges the changes of nature, and, grateful, to its parent
renders the mutual rights of service.
And by its example it reminds us to seek such friends
as not even the last day may part from our bond.
One deprived of sight carries a lame man raised on his shoulders,
and he repays his companion for these gifts with his eyes.
What each lacks, the other thus supplies in concord:
this one lends eyes, that one lends feet.
Two dangers I diligently escaped by one and the same arms,
when I was hard pressed on land, and when I was hard pressed at sea.
The shield kept me unharmed in battle; the same,
when I was shipwrecked and grasped it, carried me to the shore.
Three Graces (Charites) attend on Venus and follow their mistress,
and from this they provide pleasures and nourishment.
Joy is Euphrosyne, beautiful brightness Aglaia,
Pithus is Persuasion (Suadela), and charm of speech, caressing.
Why are they naked? Because loveliness consists in brightness
of mind, and pleases by its outstanding simplicity.
Or is it because the ungrateful return nothing, and the little chest
of the Graces is empty? He who gives presents goes naked and in need.
Why have winged sandals lately been added to their feet? He gives twice
who gives quickly. A slow favour is of very little worth.
Why, with arms entwined, is one turned away? The grateful man
lends at interest: for him, when one goes away, two remain.
Jupiter is their father; Eurynome bore the goddesses,
welcome to all, from the seed of heaven.
Whip-bearing chamber-pots and stupid schoolmasters dare
to vomit against me the bile of their impure breasts.
What shall I do? Shall I pay them back? But will it not be said
that I have seized a noisy cicada by one wing?
What use is it to drive off flies with laborious fanning?
It is better to ignore what you cannot destroy.
At night a dog looks at the moon's disc (as into a mirror),
and seeing itself, believes that there is another dog up there,
and barks: but the useless voice is driven in vain by the winds,
and deaf Diana completes her course.

162.motto: Some harm from a harmful neighbour.

reading: A torrent was sweeping along two pots, of which one was of metal,
the other made of earth by the potter's hand.
So the first asks the other whether it would be carried next to it,
so that, joined, both might withstand the rushing waters.
To it the earthen one: “I have no care for your company,
lest this nearness bring me many evils.
For whether the wave dashes you against me or me against you,
I, fragile, alone shall be broken, while you stay safe.”

163.motto: On one who perished through the savagery of his own.

reading: The surge has driven me, a dolphin, onto the shore against my will,
an example of how great are the dangers on the faithless sea.
For if Neptune does not spare even his own nurslings,
who would think that men are safe in ships?

164.motto: Εχθρῶν ἄδωρα δῶρα (“The gifts of enemies are no gifts”). On the gifts of enemies.

reading: They say that shield-bearing Ajax and Trojan Hector
received memorials of war from each other in turn.
The belt the son of Priam, the hard sword the son of Telamon:
each received the instrument of his own death.
For the sword killed Ajax, and Hector, when dead,
the belt tied to the Haemonian wheels dragged along.
So the gifts that enemies send to enemies under the name
of courtesy bring a fate that foresees what is to come.

greek.translation: The gifts of enemies are no gifts.

165.motto: One must fear even the smallest.

reading: The beetle wages war and challenges the enemy unprovoked;
inferior in strength, he overcomes by cunning.
For secretly and unrecognised he hides in the eagle's feathers,
so as to reach the enemy's nest through the high stars.
And, piercing the eggs, he prevents the hope of offspring from growing,
and, having in this way avenged the insult done to him, he departs.
The gilt-head snatches the little sardines in the middle of the sea,
unless they flee in fear and make for the surface of the sea.
But there they are food for divers and greedy coots.
Alas, weakness remains unsafe everywhere.
The others will fall mute, and the sheepskin will be silent,
if drums made from a wolf's hide sound.
The membrane of sheepskin so dreads it as an enemy
that, lifeless, it cannot bear the lifeless one.
So Cischas [Žižka], his skin stripped off and turned into a drum,
was able to defeat the Bohemian prelates.
While the Cyclops sits in the mouth of his winding cave,
he sings these words to himself among the tender sheep:
“You graze on grass; I shall feed on the Achaean comrades,
and last of all my entrails will receive Utis (“Nobody”).”
The Ithacan heard this, and made the Cyclops
bereft of sight. See how the author gets his own punishment?
A raven was carrying into the winged air a scorpion seized in its claw,
a prize won by its bold gullet.
But the scorpion, gradually pouring venom through its limbs,
as avenger drove the robber into the Stygian waters.
O thing worthy of laughter: he who was preparing death for others
himself perishes, and fell by his own wiles.

170.motto: The guilt of the offender and of the instigator is equal.

reading: A herald who had blown the battle-call on the lituus,
the victorious crowd holds captive in a gloomy prison.
He excuses himself to them, saying that he is not strong in arms
and has wounded no one's side with a cruel sword.
To him they say: “On the contrary, you yourself, most cowardly, sin more,
you who rouse others to arms with the clang of bronze.”
As a puppy seizes a stone and worries it with its bite,
but does no harm in return to the one who threw it,
so many let their true enemies slip away,
and attack with their teeth those whom no guilt burdens.
In the midst of a bristly herd stood sword-bearing Ajax,
slaughtering swine, and believing that he was slaughtering the sons of Tantalus.
So the swine, as a substitute victim, paid the penalty
for the son of Laertes and for [his] trap [?].
Madness does not know how to harm its enemies; it misses its stroke,
and, powerless in counsel, rushes to its own ruin.
The elephant (barrus), with tower-bearing shoulders and a tusk of ivory,
who is wont, fierce, to prevail in the wars of Mars,
has now put his neck under the yoke, and, subdued by goads,
draws the chariots of the Caesars to the holy temples.
Even a beast recognises that the nations everywhere are in concord,
and, with arms thrown aside, performs the duties of peace.
Behold the helmet which a fearless soldier had worn, and which
was often spattered with enemy blood.
Now that peace has been won, it has been given up to the bees for use
as a narrow hive, and it carries honeycombs and pleasant honey.
Let arms lie far away: let it be right to take up war only then
when you cannot otherwise enjoy the art of peace.
Weave slender garlands from large ears of grain,
around which let the vine go with alternating branch.
Adorned with these, the halcyons on the wave of the calm marble [sea]
build their nests and warm their still unfledged chicks.
The year will be joyful for Ceres, and fruitful for Bacchus too,
if the king is like the sea-bird.

176.motto: It is a sin for the learned to revile the learned.

reading: Why, alas, cruel Procne, do you snatch the singing cicada,
and prepare dreadful dishes for your children?
Chirping, you harm one who chirps; native, a native; guest, a guest;
feathered bird, a winged creature?
So throw away this prey: for to musical souls it is the greatest
sin for one to perish by the tooth of another.
The left hand holds a bow, the right carries a stiff club,
and the Nemean lion covers the naked body.
This, then, is the figure of Hercules. But this does not fit,
that he is old and has temples white with age.
What of the fact that his tongue is pierced with light chains,
by which he draws compliant men by their pierced ears?
Is it because the Gauls say that Alcides, excelling by his tongue,
not by strength, gave laws to the peoples?
Arms yield to the toga, and even the hardest hearts
the man powerful in eloquence draws to his wishes.
As an antidote against the drugged cups of Aeaean Circe
Mercury, the story goes, gave this to the Ithacan.
They call it moly; it is hardly pulled up by its black root;
[it is] purple, but its flower has the look of milk.
Brightness of speech and eloquence attract everyone,
but so great a thing is a work of much labour.

179.motto: All the most ancient things are fictions.

reading: Old man of Pallene, Proteus, whose form is that of an actor,
you who bear now the limbs of a man, now the limbs of a beast,
come, tell me, what reason turns you into all shapes,
so that you, ever changing, have no fixed figure?
“I display the signs of antiquity and of the primeval age,
about which each man dreams according to his own fancy.”
There are those who bear family shields with the bird of Jupiter,
there are those whose arms bear a serpent or a lion.
But let these dread animals flee from the wax [seals] of poets,
and let the beautiful swan support learned arms.
He is sacred to Phoebus and a nursling of our region;
once a king, he still keeps his ancient titles.

181.motto: Music is a care to the gods.

reading: To you, Delphic Phoebus, Eunomus of Locri set up
this cicada, a fitting sign of his victory.
He was competing with the plectrum, matched against his rival Sparthis,
and the strings struck by his thumb were giving out sound.
When a worn string (fides) began to screech with a hoarse buzz
and to spoil the lawful melody of the harmony,
then the sweet winged creature, chirping, came onto the lyre,
the cicada, to fill up the broken string with its voice.
And, drawn by the law of the sound, it came down from the high
woods, so that, chattering, it might bring us help.
So, that the honour of your cicada (O holy one) may stand firm,
here on the lyre sits she herself, a bronze lyre-player [?].

182.motto: The letter kills, the spirit gives life.

reading: When Cadmus entrusted the viper's teeth to the fields
and sowed the dread seeds in the Aonian soil,
there arose a shield-bearing cohort of earth-born men,
who fell at each other's hostile hands.
To those who escaped, on the advice of Tritonis, having thrown down
their arms, peace was given, and right hands were joined.
The son of Agenor [Cadmus] first handed down letters and signs to teachers,
and joined to them sweet harmony.
Their pupils are troubled by a great many contradictions,
which are resolved only by the help of Pallas.

183.motto: The sayings of the Seven Sages.

reading: Have these things, you who wish to portray the sayings of the Seven Sages,
and to celebrate them in pictures.
“Measure is best in all things” (as Cleobulus says):
this the tongue of the balance or the level teaches.
Chilon the Spartan bade each man know himself:
mirrors and glasses taken in the hands will show this.
What Periander of Corinth says, “Put a bridle on anger”:
pennyroyal applied to the nostrils will bring this about.
But Pittacus said, “Nothing too much”. The same is said
by those who with contracted mouth melt [?] gith.
Solon bids us look to the end: the last [limit] of the fields,
Terminus, would not yield even to great Jupiter.
Alas, how truly Bias [said], “Great is the number of the bad”:
make a Sardinian horseman sit upon a mouflon.
“Do not stand surety,” said Thales: so the parra, smeared with lime,
and the bee-eater (merops) draw their companion into snares.
What monster is this? It is the Sphinx. Why does she have the white face of a maiden,
and the feathers of birds, and the legs of a lion?
Ignorance of things has taken on this form: for of so great
an evil there is a threefold cause and origin.
Some are made ignorant by a light wit, some by caressing pleasure,
and some by proud hearts.
But those who know what the Delphic word can do
cut the dread throat of the headlong monster.
For man himself is two-footed, and three-footed, and also four-footed,
and the first laurel of the wise is to know man.
A fox, entering the workshop of a chorus-master,
found a skilfully finished human head,
so elegantly made that only breath
was lacking; in all else it would have come alive.
When she had taken it in her hands, she said:
“What a head this is, but it has no brain!”
Phrixus swims across the waters, sitting on the precious fleece,
and fearlessly mounts the golden sheep across the sea.
What does this mean? A man of dull sense but rich treasure,
whom the will of his wife or his slave rules.
Behold a girl joined to her husband by the right hand. Behold
how she sits, how a puppy plays at her feet!
This is the image of faith; but if the ardour of Venus rears it,
a branch of apples will not be amiss in her left hand.
For apples are Venus's: so Hippomenes conquered
Schoeneis; so Galathea sought her man [pelting him with an apple].
When the viper rages with desire, it stops on the shore of the sea,
and vomits dire venom from its stomach,
and, summoning the moray, raises great hissings;
and she at once seeks her husband's embraces.
The greatest reverence is owed to the marriage bed; a spouse
owes the other spouse a mutual compliance too.
As a plaything for boys throwing stones, country care
has set me, a walnut tree, at the crossroads.
Lofty, with torn branches and stripped bark,
I am pelted with slings in rivalry on every side.
What more shameful could befall a barren tree? Alas,
unhappy me: I bear fruit to my own harm.
Before the day of spring, the grey wood pigeon
builds her nest in the northern cold and warms her early eggs;
and so that the chicks may lie more softly, she plucks her own wings,
and, naked, she herself dies in the winter frost.
Is the Colchian woman not ashamed, or you, wicked Procne, when
a bird meets death for love of her own offspring?

191.motto: The piety of children towards their parents.

reading: When Aeneas was carrying from the fire, through the midst of his country's enemies,
the sweet burden of his father on his shoulders,
he said: “Have mercy! Seizing an old man will bring you no
glory; but rescuing my father will bring me the highest.”

192.motto: A woman's reputation, not her beauty, should be made public.

reading: Kindly Venus, what is this figure, what does that
tortoise mean, which you, goddess, press with your soft foot?
So Phidias portrayed me, and ordered that the female sex
should be represented by our image.
And because girls ought to stay at home and be silent,
he put such signs beneath my feet.
Betrothed Penelope wished to follow Ulysses,
had not her father Icarius preferred to keep her with him.
The one offers Ithaca, the other Sparta. The maiden remains anxious:
on this side her father's love, on that her husband's mutual love presses her.
So, sitting, she veils her face and covers her eyes:
these were the signs of bashful modesty.
By them Icarius knew that Ulysses was preferred to himself,
and in this form he set up an altar to Modesty.

194.motto: A bride married to a diseased man.

reading: “May the gods grant better to the pious! (Mezentius) why, come, do you
address me so? Because a son-in-law has been bought by you with a dowry,
whom the dread French scab and chin-rash (mentagra) burn up:
what else is this (tell me, cruel father)
than joining bodies to bodies, the dead to the living,
and renewing the savage deeds of the Etruscan leader?”
The image of the turning-post and the name of the cypress show
that one's own are to be treated on equal terms.

epigrams.label: Another.
reading: The cypress is a funeral tree: the monuments of nobles it,
as parsley those of the common people, is wont to adorn with its leaves.

epigrams.label: Another.
reading: Beautiful is the foliage, and the leaves are arranged in beautiful order,
but this beautiful foliage bears no fruits.
The oak is pleasing to Jupiter, who both preserves and cherishes us:
to him who saves a citizen an oaken crown is given.

epigrams.label: Another.
reading: With acorns it fed the ancients; now it is useful by its shade alone:
so in this way too, in this way too, the tree of Jupiter is obliging.
Because Homer called the willow “fruit-destroying”,
it likens to itself men of the manners of Clitor.
The fir, fit for the seas, grows on high mountains:
and in adversity there is the greatest advantage.
But the spruce, because it sends out no shoots from its root,
is a sign of him who perishes without offspring.
Ancient Solon is said to have decreed
that Cydonian apples [quinces] ought to be given to newly-weds,
since they are pleasing to mouth and stomach, so that their breath too
may be sweet, and a caressing charm may stay on their lips.
The never-withering little shrub of ivy, which, they say,
Bacchus gave as a gift to the boy Cissus:
straying, wanton, tawny with golden clusters,
green on the outside, the rest has pallor.
Hence poets bind their temples with fitting garlands:
they grow pale from study, their praise stays green for long.
Because the holm oak splits itself through excessive hardness,
it bears the symbols of civil sedition.
These are the golden apples of Venus: their pleasant bitterness
shows it; so among the Greeks love is γλυκυπίκρος (“bittersweet”).
The ever-green box with its curly top,
from which the pipe of unequal measures is made,
is a tree suited to tender delights and to lovers.
There is pallor in it, and every lover is pale.
But the late mulberry never buds until the cold
has passed, and, wise, it bears a false name (morus — μωρός, “foolish”).
Why, almond tree, in your haste do you send out your flowers before your leaves?
I hate children of precocious wit.
The laurel, foreknowing the future, bears signs of coming good fortune.
Placed under the pillow, it makes dreams come true.

epigrams.label: Another.
reading: The laurel crown is owed to Charles for conquering the Carthaginians:
let such garlands adorn victorious hair.
In that the two-coloured poplar adorns the hair of Hercules,
[it is shown that] night and day alternate the changes of time.
